blocks.text: When macrophages attack invading microbes they release chemicals called pyrogens. These travel in the blood to the brain and reach the hypothalamus, the body's thermostat, where they make it raise the body's core temperature above the normal 37 C (98.6 F). A higher-than-normal temperature is fever (pyrexia).

blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: macrophages attack microbes; they release pyrogens into the blood; the hypothalamus, the body's thermostat, raises the set point; fever above 37 C (98.6 F). A box below lists the effects of fever and the dangerous temperatures.
blocks.caption: How fever is set off and what it does (original flow diagram for this topic).
blocks.long_description: When macrophages attack invading microbes they release pyrogens, which travel in the blood to the hypothalamus, the body's thermostat, and make it raise the core temperature above the normal 37 C (98.6 F): fever, or pyrexia. Fever hinders the reproduction of bacteria and viruses, kills some temperature-sensitive microbes, speeds up neutrophils and macrophages and increases the release of cytokines such as interferons. Temperatures above about 103 F (39.4 C) are considered dangerous, and above about 105 F (40.5 C) are often fatal.

items: Fever hinders the reproduction of bacteria and viruses.
Some temperature-sensitive microbes, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and influenza virus, are killed at high fever.
Fever speeds up the action of neutrophils and macrophages.
During fever the body releases more cytokines (interferons).

blocks.title: For information: when fever is dangerous
blocks.text: In general, temperatures above 103 F (39.4 C) are considered dangerous, and those above 105 F (40.5 C) are often fatal.

blocks.prompt: Trace the path from a macrophage to a fever.
blocks.explanation: Macrophages attacking microbes release pyrogens; these reach the hypothalamus through the blood; the hypothalamus raises the body's set temperature, causing fever.

items: Pyrogens from macrophages reset the hypothalamus above 37 C.
Fever slows microbes and speeds phagocytes; above 103 F dangerous, above 105 F often fatal.
